newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New ISM safety rules to disrupt shipping - ABS.
newsitem.headline: New ISM safety rules to disrupt shipping - ABS.

text.p: The shipping industry could face disruption next year when new safety rules become mandatory as only some eight percent of vessels have won certification so far, the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) said on Tuesday.

Ravinder Chadha of the U.S.-based classification society said about 19,000 ships and 8,000 firms need certification of compliance with the International Management Code for Safe Operation of Ships and Pollution Prevention, or ISM.
"Of these, approximately 1,600 vessels and 550 companies have achieved certification so far," Chadha said in a speech prepared for delivery to the Asia Pacific Ship Management conference,
"With only a year left to the deadline, the approximately 500 plus auditors available with the Classification Societies cannot even hope to complete certificate audits."

Certification becomes mandatory on July 1, 1998 for passenger ships, bulk carriers, tankers and high speed craft registered in the more than 130 countries which ratified the 1974 International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea
The code will be extended to other types of vessels and mobile offshore drilling units by July 1, 2002.

The ISM Code, adopted by the International Maritime Organisation in 1994, aims to ensure safety at sea and avoid damage to the environment by requiring ships officers and managers vessels to develop, implement and assess pollution prevention measurea according to a set of specific guidelines.
Chadha appealed to shipping company managers to start seeking certification "immediately" as the normal implementation period can take 12-14 months.

In the absence of a valid certificate on board the vessel, port state authorities, including the U.S. Coast Guard, would investigate conditions thoroughly, leading to possible delays or detentions, Chandha said.
"No one in authority is talking of relaxation as of this date as yet," he said.

"As a result, perfectly safe vessels run the risk of detention due to inadequate SOLAS certification. If port states choose to apply sanctions, then the shipping industry is sure to witness some disruptions."
